place: A frozen pond at the edge of the homestead, the ice thin near a spring that keeps the water moving underneath.
lines: I climb out and run for the house
I strip off my wet clothes and put on the dry wool by the fire
outcome: The ice gives way and the player goes in to the waist, soaking coat and boots in freezing water. Running home keeps them moving, but the wet wool clings and drags heat out fast; stripping it off for dry wool and the fire lets them warm back up over the next while, shivering hard but recovering. Staying in the wet clothes by the fire instead would have kept sapping warmth even next to the flames, and the shivering would have gotten worse rather than better.

numbers: how much weight the ice can bear before it fails
how fast body heat leaves wet skin in moving cold air

effects: moves wet wool coat to peg
numbers: how long until shivering stops
how long by the fire before warmth returns to normal

latent: whether the spring keeps a patch of ice thin every winter in the same spot
state_after: player: dry, warm again, tired
wet wool coat: soaked, drying by the fire
pond ice: broken near the spring
stress: wet insulation actively pulls heat out even near a fire, so drying is not optional
temptation: a special rule for 'pond ice near the spring is dangerous' instead of a general thinness-of-ice property

place: The homestead yard during a wet, near-freezing drizzle that turns to sleet by evening.
outcome: The linen shirt worn under the coat soaks through almost at once in the sleet and clings cold to the skin, doing almost nothing to hold warmth once wet. The wool coat over it helps some, since wool keeps some loft even damp, but the player stays chilled at the chest where the wet linen touches skin. By the time the wood is stacked they are shivering and slow to warm back up.

numbers: how quickly linen saturates in sleet of that intensity
how much heat a wet layer against skin draws away
how much a damp wool layer slows further heat loss compared to dry

latent: that the wool coat was already slightly damp from the morning and would have wet through fully given more time
state_after: linen shirt: soaked, cold against skin
wool coat: damp but still lofted
player: chilled at chest, shivering, wood stacked
stress: a fabric's insulating property, not the fabric itself, and how wetness cancels it differently per material
temptation: a rule that 'linen is bad, wool is good' instead of wetness interacting with thickness and loft

place: A one-room timber house at night with a stone hearth, one shutter warped and leaving a gap at its edge.
outcome: The wind rises overnight and finds the gap at the warped shutter, driving a thin stream of freezing air across the room that the fire cannot counter because a fire heats the air, it does not stop a draft. Even banked well, the fire cannot keep the side of the room nearest the gap warm, and whoever sleeps closest wakes stiff and cold while those on the far side stay fine. Nobody notices the cause until morning light shows frost on the inside wall by the shutter.

numbers: how much cold air moves through a gap of that size per hour
how much colder the near side of the room gets than the far side

effects: family learns cause of the cold
numbers: how low the surface temperature must fall for frost to form indoors

latent: that the shutter has been warped since autumn and nobody fixed it
state_after: warped shutter: still gapped
wall near shutter: frosted
family member nearest the gap: cold, stiff
hearth fire: burned to embers, undiminished effect on the draft
stress: heat and draft are separate things; a fire raises air temperature but does not stop moving air, so a gap can beat a fire
temptation: a rule specific to 'the warped shutter causes cold' instead of any gap letting outside air through a barrier

place: A hunting shelter of piled stone and brush, one small fire near the open entrance, no door.
outcome: The fire is not fed and burns down over the night while the hunter sleeps. The wool bedroll holds some warmth, but the open entrance lets cold night air pool in as the fire's heat fades, and by the coldest hour before dawn the hunter is curled tight and shivering in their sleep without waking fully. They wake stiff, slow to think, clumsy with their hands, and sharply hungry, and have burned through a good part of the wood for no lasting effect since nobody woke to add more.

numbers: how long a given pile of wood burns unattended
how far body temperature drifts over a full night without a fire
how long stiffness and slow thinking last after waking cold

latent: how much wood was actually left unburned that could have been added
state_after: small fire: out, embers only
hunter: cold, stiff, slow, hungry, warming up
firewood pile: mostly consumed
stress: unattended fuel runs out on its own schedule; nobody typing does not mean nothing happens
temptation: a rule that 'sleeping by a fire keeps you warm' as a flat fact rather than fuel and time interacting

place: The homestead well-yard at dawn, all metal fittings rimed with frost, air well below freezing.
lines: I grab the iron bucket handle with my bare hands to haul it up
outcome: Bare skin against frost-covered iron loses heat far faster than against wood or rope, since metal carries heat away from the hand quickly, and within a short time the fingers gripping the handle go numb and white at the tips. The player can still work for a while without feeling it, which is itself the danger, and only notices when the fingers no longer bend properly. Warming them slowly indoors brings back stinging and colour; warming them fast against the stove would hurt worse and risk the skin.

numbers: how fast bare skin loses heat to frosted metal versus wood
how long before numbness sets in at that temperature
how far below freezing and how long before tissue is harmed
how long safe slow rewarming takes

latent: that the fingertips are pale rather than merely cold, meaning early frostbite rather than simple chill
state_after: bare hands: warmed, stinging, fingertips tender
iron bucket handle: still frosted
player: aware to wear gloves next time
stress: metal draws heat from skin much faster than other materials at the same temperature, and numbness hides the injury as it happens
temptation: a rule 'touching iron in winter causes frostbite' instead of general heat conduction plus exposure time

place: An open snowfield above the treeline, cloudless midday sun reflecting off unbroken snow.
lines: I walk across the open snow to check the ridge for game
outcome: The sun reflects off the flat snow into the player's eyes for hours with nothing shading them, and though nothing feels wrong at the time, by evening the eyes feel gritty and start to ache, worsening overnight into real pain and blurred, watery vision. It is not a wound anyone dealt but light and glare doing slow damage that shows up late. Resting the eyes in a dark room over the following day eases it; going back out into bright snow before that would make it worse.

numbers: how many hours of glare exposure it takes to injure the eyes
delay between exposure and symptoms starting
how many hours until pain peaks
how many days of rest the eyes need to recover

latent: that the ache building through the afternoon was already the injury starting, not just tiredness
state_after: player: eyes aching, vision blurred, resting indoors
open snowfield: unchanged
stress: damage from light and glare accumulates with exposure time and shows up only after a delay
temptation: a rule 'snow causes blindness' instead of glare exposure over time versus eye protection

place: The woodpile behind the house, cold and still, no wind.
lines: I chop wood for an hour
I stop to rest against the shed wall
outcome: An hour of hard chopping in a heavy wool coat works the player hot enough to sweat under the wool, and they open the coat to cool off as they work. The moment they stop and lean against the shed wall to rest, the sweat-damp shirt against skin starts pulling heat away in the still cold air, and within a short while they are shivering harder than before they started, colder than if they had never worked up a sweat at all. Closing the coat and moving again brings the warmth back, but resting still in sweat-damp clothes was the mistake.

numbers: how long hard labor takes to produce a sweat in cold air
how fast a damp shirt chills a resting body compared to a dry one
how long moving again takes to restore warmth

latent: that the shirt was wetter under the arms and back than the player realized while still working
state_after: player: warmed again, tired, shirt still damp under the coat
log pile: reduced
axe: put away
stress: exertion and rest reverse the effect of a wet layer: helpful while moving, dangerous once still
temptation: a rule 'sweating is good, resting is good' as flat facts instead of wetness plus stillness plus cold air

place: The homestead over three cold, damp days following a soaking in freezing rain.
outcome: After a soaking in freezing rain that was shrugged off at the time, the player keeps working in clothes that never fully dry through, and over the following two days a persistent chill that will not shake off turns into aches, then a fever with sweats and shivering by turns. Nothing dramatic happens on any single day; it is the accumulation of unresolved cold and damp that finally overwhelms the body. Rest, warmth and dry bedding over several more days bring the fever down, but pushing through chores sick would have made it worse and slower to pass.

numbers: how long the rain lasted
how many days of incomplete drying before illness sets in
delay between the soaking and the fever appearing
how many days of rest the fever takes to break

latent: that the clothes never actually dried through despite looking dry on the outside
state_after: player: feverish then recovering, in bed
damp clothes: finally dried and put away
freezing rain: long since passed
stress: illness here is an accumulation over days, not an event, and shrugging off the original cause does not prevent it
temptation: a rule 'getting rained on causes fever' instead of unresolved wet and cold compounding over days of continued exertion

place: The well at the edge of the yard, its surface iced over, the bucket rope stiff with frost.
lines: I break the ice on the well and haul up a bucket
I carry it back to the house
outcome: Breaking the surface ice takes real effort, and the rope, stiff with its own frost, is awkward to haul on, so the bucket comes up unevenly and slops water over the rim onto the player's sleeve and glove on the way up. In the cold air that splash freezes onto the wool almost as fast as it lands, turning a small spill into a stiff, ice-crusted cuff that chafes and chills the wrist by the time they reach the house. The water itself makes it back mostly full.

numbers: how much force breaks ice of that thickness

effects: transfers water from well to bucket
numbers: how much water is lost hauling unevenly
how fast a splash freezes onto fabric in that air

latent: that the rope's stiffness, not the ice, was what actually caused the spill
state_after: well: open at the broken patch, will refreeze by morning
wool sleeve: ice-crusted, chafing
bucket: mostly full, carried inside
stress: a small, one-time spill becomes a lasting problem once the cold locks it in place as ice
temptation: a rule 'wells freeze in winter' instead of the rope's stiffness and the spill's fate in cold air

place: The path between the house and the barn, glazed with a hard sheet of ice under a light dusting of snow that hides it.
lines: I carry the feed sack out to the barn
outcome: The path looks merely snowy but is ice underneath, and the weight of the feed sack thrown off balance is enough to put the player down hard when a foot slides out from under them. They catch themselves badly and the ankle twists under the fall, swelling almost at once and refusing to bear weight properly. For the rest of the day and into the next, carrying, climbing and fast walking are all out of reach, and chores that need two good legs have to wait or be done differently.

numbers: how much snow it takes to hide ice from sight
how much off-balance weight increases the chance of a fall
how long the ankle needs before it bears weight again
how many days the limitation lasts

latent: that the whole path, not just this one spot, is glazed under the snow
state_after: player: ankle swollen, limping, resting weight off it
feed sack: dropped, recovered
icy path: still hidden under snow elsewhere
stress: a hidden hazard plus an unbalancing load compounds into an injury with effects that outlast the moment
temptation: a rule 'the path near the barn is icy' instead of hidden ice plus load plus balance

place: The homestead kitchen over several days of hard frost, hands going in and out to the yard repeatedly.
outcome: Over several days the player's hands go from bitter cold outdoor air to the direct heat of the hearth and back again many times a day, warming too fast each time rather than gradually. Neither the cold alone nor the heat alone is the problem; it is the repeated swing between them that leaves small blood vessels in the fingers unable to keep up, and by the third or fourth day the fingertips turn red then purplish, swollen and maddeningly itchy, worse in the warm and only somewhat eased in the cold. It is not an injury from any one moment but from the pattern repeated, and it will keep recurring each cold snap.

numbers: how many trips outside per day
how quickly the hands go from cold to hot each time
how many days of cycling before chilblains appear

latent: that it is the repetition and speed of the swing, not the cold or the heat alone, that caused it
state_after: hands: fingertips reddened, swollen, itching
player: avoiding sudden reheating near the hearth
stress: harm from a pattern repeated over days rather than any single exposure, and from too-fast reheating rather than cold itself
temptation: a rule 'cold hands get chilblains' instead of the cycling speed and repetition doing the damage

place: The one-room house on the coldest week of winter, a goat brought in from the freezing barn.
lines: I bring the goat inside for the night
outcome: Bringing the goat in out of a barn too cold to be safe for it adds a second warm body's worth of heat to the small room, noticeably easing how much wood the fire needs to keep it comfortable. But the goat is not a small cost: it eats through stored hay meant to last, and left loose it fouls the floor and knocks over anything within reach, so the household trades some firewood and comfort for cleanup and diminished feed stores. Over a hard enough winter the trade is still worth it for the animal's survival, but it is not free.

numbers: how much one animal's body heat raises a small room's temperature
how much hay a goat eats overnight indoors
how much mess accumulates overnight

latent: whether the barn was actually cold enough that night to risk the goat's life by leaving it there
state_after: goat: warm, fed, indoors
house: warmer, floor fouled
hay store: reduced
stress: a benefit shared body heat brings that comes bundled with unavoidable costs, not a clean trade
temptation: a rule 'goats warm houses' instead of body heat, consumption and mess as separate general effects of an animal indoors

place: The yard and the path to the woodshed, a light snow falling, a child sent to fetch kindling.
outcome: The child, smaller and losing heat faster for their size than an adult would, gets absorbed in play in the snow on the way back and loses track of time, staying out far longer than the errand needed. Nobody notices right away because the errand seemed short and simple; by the time the child comes in, shivering hard, clumsy-fingered and unable to explain clearly what took so long, they are already colder than an adult would be after the same time outside, and warming them back up safely takes real care rather than just standing them by the fire at once.

numbers: how much longer than the errand the child actually stayed out
how much faster a small body loses heat than an adult's in the same cold

effects: player learns child is too cold
numbers: how late the delay in noticing pushed the cold before anyone acted
how long safe gradual rewarming of a child takes

latent: that the child had been sitting still building a snow shape rather than moving, which cooled them faster than walking would have
state_after: child: warming slowly, shivering easing, tired
kindling: eventually brought in, less than needed
player: resolving to set a shorter watch on errands
stress: body size changes the rate of heat loss, and a short errand can silently become a dangerous exposure
temptation: a rule 'children get cold faster' as a flat fact instead of size affecting heat loss rate combined with an unwatched delay

place: The barnyard at dusk, a startled ox knocking the player back against the fence rail.
outcome: The ox, spooked by something in the cold dark, swings its weight into the player and knocks them back hard into the fence rail. The thick hide coat the player wears against the cold happens to take most of the force across the ribs and back, spreading and softening the blow enough that nothing breaks, but a solid bruise blooms under the coat by evening and stays sore for days, aching worse in the cold. Without the coat's padding the same blow would likely have cracked a rib rather than just bruised one.

numbers: how likely a startled ox is to bolt or swing
how much force the ox's weight delivers
how much force a thick padded layer spreads compared to bare cloth
how many days the bruise takes to stop aching in cold weather

latent: that a rib came close to cracking and only the coat's padding kept it from fully breaking
state_after: player: bruised ribs, sore, moving carefully
thick hide coat: dented but intact
ox: calmed
stress: a padded layer's thickness converts a break into a bruise by spreading force, not by magic protection
temptation: a rule 'the hide coat protects against ox kicks' instead of general force-spreading by thickness and padding

place: The house at night, a trapper coming in from hours checking snares with fingers gone hard and white.
lines: I shove my hands right up close to the fire to warm them fast
outcome: The fingers came in already hard, white and numb from hours in the cold, true frostbite rather than simple chill, and shoving them right up to the open flame to warm them as fast as possible feels like the obvious fix. But fast, uneven heat against tissue that is frozen through causes worse damage than slow, even warming would: the skin reddens unevenly, blisters rise where the heat was too close, and the pain when feeling returns is far sharper than it would have been from gentler warming in water kept just pleasantly warm. The fingers end up more damaged for having been rushed.

numbers: how many hours of that cold it takes to freeze tissue through
how much closer than safe the fingers were held
how much worse the pain and damage are from fast versus slow rewarming

latent: that a basin of warm, not hot, water sitting nearby would have rewarmed the fingers safely
state_after: frostbitten fingers: blistered, painful, clumsy
open fire: unchanged
player: aware too late of the warm water option
stress: the rate and evenness of rewarming matters as much as reaching warmth at all, and fast is not simply better
temptation: a rule 'warm frostbite by the fire' instead of general harm from fast, uneven heat applied to frozen tissue
